title: The Mishnah
hookLine: six orders of oral teaching, written down so they wouldn't be lost

lines: SONS HOME LATE FROM A WEDDING.
cards: The book begins with a question, and not a grand one. From when may a person recite the Shema in the evening? No creation story.
No hero. Just a practical question about a prayer said every night, and right away three answers: Rabbi Eliezer says one thing, the sages another, Rabban Gamaliel a third. Then a little story.
Gamaliel's sons come home late from a wedding feast and tell their father they haven't said the Shema yet. The night is far along. Is it too late?
That is how the Mishnah opens: a family, a late night, and a room full of teachers who don't all agree.

teach.h: ORAL TORAH, NOW ON THE PAGE.
teach.b: The Mishnah is teaching that tradition calls oral Torah: the explanation that, in Jewish belief, traveled alongside the written Torah, taught teacher to student and learned by heart.
Tradition ties the name to a Hebrew word for repeating, because it was learned by saying it over and over. Now it is written.

teach.h: SIX ORDERS, FOUND IN ONE VERSE.
teach.b: Six orders, each called a seder. The Talmud later finds all six in a single verse of Isaiah, one word for each: seeds and farming, appointed times and festivals, women and marriage, damages, holy things, and purities.
Inside the orders are tractates, inside the tractates chapters, and inside each chapter short units, each also called a mishnah. So the word names the whole book and one small piece of it.
What surprises a first reader is that the Mishnah keeps the minority opinion. Back to that first page. The sages say the evening Shema may be said until midnight.
Rabban Gamaliel says until dawn. So when his sons come home late, he tells them: if the dawn hasn't come up, you are still obliged to say it. And the page records both views, with names attached.
Disagreement isn't erased when the teaching is written down. It's kept, carefully, as part of the teaching. The oral, written, still sounds like people talking.

how: Jews study Mishnah in small portions, and some learn a chapter in memory of someone who has died; it is studied in yeshivas, synagogues and at home, often aloud with a partner.

games.q: you're Rabban Gamaliel. your sons come home late at night from a wedding feast and haven't said the evening Shema. what do you tell them?
o: it's late, so it's too late tonight.
if dawn hasn't come up, you're still obliged to say it.
skip it and say two tomorrow.
games.why: he tells them that until the dawn comes up, they are still obliged to say it. the Mishnah keeps his view right beside the sages' midnight.

practice: Here is the first mishnah in plain words. From when may the Shema be said in the evening? From the hour the priests go in to eat their holy portion; until when?
Rabbi Eliezer says until the end of the first watch of the night, the sages say until midnight, and Rabban Gamaliel says until dawn.
Hold the three answers side by side, nobody erased, and if you pray, say a short evening prayer you know; if not, rest with the question: what in your life is still not too late?
